quick: With or without food; separate from cations
Use only if benefit outweighs risk
No adjustment in mild-moderate; caution in severe
QT/ECG if at risk; tendon, glucose, CNS effects
summary: Moxifloxacin is a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibacterial with enhanced Gram-positive and anaerobic activity, used once daily (400 mg) for respiratory, skin, intra-abdominal and other infections, and for plague. It carries class boxed warnings for disabling and potentially irreversible tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects and exacerbation of myasthenia gravis, plus a notable risk of QT prolongation. Reserve for situations without alternative options where appropriate.
indications: Acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis
Uncomplicated and complicated skin and skin-structure infections
Plague (treatment and prophylaxis) due to Yersinia pestis

dosage.d: 400 mg IV or PO once every 24 hours

admin: Oral tablets may be taken with or without food, at the same time each day
Separate oral dosing by at least 4 hours before or 8 hours after antacids, sucralfate, multivitamins, and products containing magnesium, aluminum, iron, zinc or calcium
IV: infuse over 60 minutes; do not give as a rapid or bolus infusion
No dose adjustment is needed for renal or mild-moderate hepatic impairment
Maintain adequate hydration to prevent concentrated urine and crystalluria
moa: Moxifloxacin inhibits the bacterial type II topoisomerases DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, enzymes essential for DNA replication, transcription, repair and recombination. Inhibition prevents supercoiling and separation of bacterial DNA, producing bactericidal activity. Its C8-methoxy structure broadens Gram-positive and anaerobic coverage and may reduce selection of resistant mutants.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to moxifloxacin or any fluoroquinolone
relative: Known QT prolongation, uncorrected hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, or concurrent class IA/III antiarrhythmics
History of tendon disorders or fluoroquinolone-associated tendinopathy
Significant bradycardia or acute myocardial ischemia
monitor: Elderly, transplant recipients, or concurrent corticosteroids (tendon rupture risk)
Seizure disorder or CNS conditions lowering seizure threshold

preg: There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Fluoroquinolones are expected to be excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the infant, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug.
renal: No dosage adjustment is required in renal impairment, including patients on hemodialysis or continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis, as nonrenal elimination predominates.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is needed in mild to moderate hepatic impairment. Pharmacokinetics in severe hepatic impairment have not been fully studied, and metabolic disturbances associated with hepatic insufficiency may increase QT-prolongation risk; use with caution.

major: Class IA (quinidine, procainamide) and class III (amiodarone, sotalol) antiarrhythmics - additive QT prolongation/torsades
Other QT-prolonging drugs (antipsychotics, macrolides, TCAs, ondansetron) - additive QT risk
moderate: Antidiabetic agents - hyper- or hypoglycemia; monitor glucose
Warfarin - enhanced anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
minor: Multivalent cation products (antacids, iron, calcium, zinc, sucralfate, didanosine) - chelation reduces absorption; separate dosing
interactions.food: Food does not significantly impair absorption, but dairy and cation-containing products/supplements reduce absorption - separate dosing.
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; avoid additive CNS effects.
interactions.diagnostics: May affect blood glucose readings (dysglycemia); can prolong QT on ECG.

monitoring: ECG/QT in patients with risk factors; correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia before therapy
Tendon pain or swelling - discontinue at first sign and avoid exercise of the affected area
Blood glucose in diabetics; signs of peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects
Liver enzymes and signs of C. difficile colitis with persistent diarrhea
counsel: Stop the drug and contact your doctor for tendon pain/swelling, numbness or tingling, palpitations or fainting
Separate doses from antacids, iron, calcium, zinc and multivitamins
Avoid excessive sun exposure (photosensitivity) and stay well hydrated
Diabetics should monitor blood sugar; report confusion, agitation or seizures
Tell your doctor about heart-rhythm problems, myasthenia gravis or prior tendon problems
pk: Store at 20-25 C; do not refrigerate IV solution
pearls: Boxed warning: disabling, potentially irreversible tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects and myasthenia gravis exacerbation - reserve for when other options are unsuitable
QT prolongation: avoid with other QT drugs and correct electrolytes first
Not adjusted for renal function, but minimal urinary concentrations make it a poor choice for simple UTIs
Watch for dysglycemia, especially in elderly diabetics on sulfonylureas/insulin
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue once-daily dosing; do not double the dose.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. In overdose, empty the stomach if appropriate, maintain hydration, and observe with ECG monitoring for QT prolongation. Treat symptomatically and supportively. Only modest amounts are removed by hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.
